purpose: Fourth Benchmark v2 case, Epic 4.3 Bucket C: a real, currently-contested research question in this project's AuDHD domain (distinct from case 2's known-open causal-mechanism question, which the literature frames as simply unresolved/uninvestigated). Here real trials and reviews exist and actively disagree with each other, not merely being sparse -- tests whether pipeline/gap_challenger.py's decision table can recognize genuine literature-internal contradiction (CONTESTED) rather than defaulting to OPEN (missing the substantial real evidence that exists) or LIKELY_CLOSED/CLOSED (falsely treating disputed efficacy/safety findings as settled).
ground_truth_note: Acceptable terminal statuses for this case: CONTESTED (correctly recognizes literature-internal disagreement) or PARTIALLY_OPEN (finds the real relevant trial/review evidence but the judge does not flag it as mutually contradicting -- a real, if softer, miss than mislabeling this OPEN or CLOSED). LIKELY_CLOSED or CLOSED would be a real miss (treating a genuinely disputed efficacy/tolerability question as resolved). OPEN would also be a real miss (failing to find the substantial existing trial/review literature that exists, e.g. RUPP 2005, Cochrane 2017). INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE is an acceptable, honest non-failure if search coverage genuinely fell below threshold that run.

gap.title: Efficacy and tolerability of stimulant medication for ADHD symptoms in children with comorbid autism spectrum disorder
gap.description: Whether methylphenidate reliably improves ADHD symptoms (hyperactivity, inattention) in children with comorbid autism spectrum disorder, at an efficacy and tolerability profile comparable to its use in ADHD without autism, is unresolved -- real trials and reviews report materially different response rates, adverse-event rates, and effects on stereotyped behavior, and a recent mini-review explicitly attributes decades of clinical hesitancy to 'conflicting data.'
gap.missing_connection: reliability and safety of stimulant medication response in comorbid autism-ADHD relative to isolated ADHD

verification.method: Real web search, 2026-08-24 -- not assumed, not generated by the pipeline under test.
verification.summary: This is real, acknowledged, ongoing disagreement in the literature, not merely sparse research. The RUPP Autism Network's randomized controlled crossover trial (2005) found a 49% clinical response rate to methylphenidate in children with pervasive developmental disorders and hyperactivity, but an 18% discontinuation rate due to adverse effects (mainly irritability) -- versus under 4% discontinuation for adverse effects among children with ADHD alone in the contemporaneous NIMH Multimodal Treatment of ADHD (MTA) study, indicating a materially different efficacy/tolerability profile in the comorbid population. The 2017 Cochrane systematic review (Sturman, Deckx & van Driel) found only a small number of small crossover trials, concluded short-term hyperactivity/inattention improvement is possible but explicitly characterized the evidence base as limited, with no clear evidence on core ASD-symptom effects or long-term safety. Most directly, a 2023 mini-review (Dimitri et al., Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry) states outright that methylphenidate's 'reliability... for the treatment of children with ASD and comorbid ADHD has been discussed over the past decades, and its employment has been hampered by conflicting data' -- explicitly contrasting earlier reports of limited efficacy and exacerbated side effects against more recent favorable findings, i.e. real researchers actively disagreeing, not a topic nobody has studied.

sources.title: Randomized, Controlled, Crossover Trial of Methylphenidate in Pervasive Developmental Disorders With Hyperactivity (RUPP Autism Network, Archives of General Psychiatry, 2005)
Methylphenidate for children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (Sturman, Deckx & van Driel, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2017)

Observing the behavioural effects of methylphenidate in children and adolescents with ASD-ADHD dual diagnosis: A mini review (Dimitri et al., Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 2023) -- explicitly describes the evidence as hampered by 'conflicting data'

notes: Chosen specifically because a real review uses the word 'conflicting' about this literature (not this project's characterization) and because a real large RCT (RUPP 2005) and a real Cochrane systematic review (2017) exist and can be checked against each other -- distinguishing this from a 'not much research exists' case, which is a different failure mode than genuine contestation.
